newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finns unlikely to rebel in EU parliament election.
newsitem.headline: Finns unlikely to rebel in EU parliament election.

text.p: Finns on Sunday become the last of the European Union's three newest national electorates to signal their mood about the bloc in polling for European Parliament seats, and outsiders may be surprised at the outcome.

"This is not a referendum on Europe," said Tuomo Martikainen, political science professor at Helsinki University. "It's typical of Finns to be pragmatic. The question of (EU) membership is past -- why worry about it?"

Unlike the Austrians last weekend and the Swedes last year, the Finns, in their first experience of a direct election for members of the Strasbourg-based parliament, may even suggest they approve of membership in the 15-nation group.

Commentators say that would only be part of the story. Apathy and indifference, as well as protest no-shows in mainly rural northern areas, are expected to reduce the turnout, typically over 70 percent in a general election, to the low 60s. Sunday's Europoll will be twinned with local council elections.

"There are a lot of people going to the polls who don't have a clue about what this is about," said Matti Morttinen, a writer at the daily newspaper Aamulehti who has followed EU issues for five years.

"This election has already been nicknamed the celebrity poll," he said, referring to the assorted sports personalities, a film maker, a television host and a gay weatherman who are among the 207 candidates nationwide for the 16 seats at stake.

With the exception of a few political heavyweights, the Euro-candidates aim to be eye-catching rather than highbrow. Real issues -- like unemployment which at 16 to 17 percent is among the highest rates in Europe -- are unlikely to arise.

Opinion polls show only a slight Euro-sceptic shift from Finland's October 1994 referendum where 57 percent voted for, 43 percent against membership, although a majority of Finns at around 60 percent oppose a planned single EU currency.

An August-September survey by the Centre for Finnish Business and Policy Studies found 71 percent of respondents felt EU membership was favourable or neutral for Finland, and less than one-tenth found it very negative.
"We are different from Austria -- Finns are quite happy with membership or at least it has been problem-free," said Pekka Karhuvaara, editor-in-chief of the populist daily Iltalehti.

Finland joined the EU with Sweden and Austria in 1995 and the perspective here is different. Membership has coincided with an end to recession and, for many Finns their country's place in the bloc is a sign that they belong in the West and cannot be leaned on by neighbouring Russia, which ruled here until 1917.
Current support for Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's Social Democrat party would also be the envy of Austria's chancellor, according to opinion polls published on Tuesday and Wednesday.

A beefy former waterpolo player who local media have pointed out bears a slight physical resemblance to Russian security chief Alexander Lebed, his party's backing in an October poll at 26.7 percent was up on August-September's 24.5 percent.
The polls also show backing for the main opposition to Lipponen's five-party ruling coalition, the Centre Party, shrinking slightly, to 20.5 percent from 21.3.

Led by former prime minister Esko Aho, the party, whose support is highest among farmers, has made some slightly Euro-doubtful statements on their behalf. But they are unconvincing -- it was Aho who took Finland into Europe in 1995. Reflecting his past majority, his party is now the biggest group in the Europarliament with five of Finland's 16 seats.
